Yet butchers and traders, instead of putting these cattle to work plowing along the Ji River, deliver them to the cooking pots of the people of Wu. Is this not because the northward journey is overland and the southward journey by water? Driving and hauling them overland is difficult and certainly cannot compare with the ease of transporting them by boat. The circumstances are readily understood, and the practice readily stopped. If just one official were appointed to oversee it, within a year cattle would be found throughout the fields. When Li Biao served under the Later Wei, he assessed the suitability of waterways and land routes, calculated the acreage, and purchased cattle with confiscated illicit proceeds and payments for redeeming punishments. People at the time relied on this to achieve abundance. During the Kaiyuan reign of the Tang, too, the suitability of the soil was assessed, and cattle were allocated in varying numbers according to whether it was soft or hard. Could any of these methods not be implemented today?
If undertakings do not follow ancient precedents, they require much labor for little result. Yet when the methods of the ancients are available and we still drift along without taking action, such is the fate of these people! If you, sir, could convey this to His Majesty, establish statutory regulations, and assess the agricultural officials’ performance as inferior or superior, while applying the four measures I have proposed, making their penalties strict and strengthening their authority, then—even if the benefits were not immediately apparent—within ten years the realm would be prosperous and populous, filled with harmonious influences. His Majesty could then compose music and establish pitch standards as he wished. Yet these proposals did not originate with me. Those of old who established the achievements of true kings or hegemons, subdued the Rong and Di, and attained the south-facing position of sovereignty with ease stand resplendent in the historical records; none failed to…

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
率由玆道況以天下之力爲之其所成就
豈曰小補之哉故愚必欲先之以貴粟終
之以重其權而後古先聖王休養生息之
道乃復見於
今日矣夫春秋於他穀不書惟禾麥不熟則
書之重民命也執事幸勿以爲迂
第三問
林一新
同考試官教諭洪批作樂在養太和否則眞
===
精散漫攝之爲難此篇以元聲元氣立言可謂知本之論
同考試官教諭沈批慨慕古樂若見其盛其
高志之士歟
同考試官教諭顏批樂理極玄學者罕喻子
論斷古今多出所見蓋留心久矣孰謂天下無鍾期乎
考試官教諭尹批知心有元聲元氣可與
言樂矣
考試官教授薛批史遷知制律之本子知
作樂之本
punctuated:
率由玆道，況以天下之力爲之，其所成就豈曰小補之哉？故愚必欲先之以貴粟，終之以重其權，而後古先聖王休養生息之道乃復見於今日矣。夫《春秋》於他穀不書，惟禾麥不熟則書之，重民命也。執事幸勿以爲迂。
第三問
林一新
同考試官教諭洪批：作樂在養太和，否則眞精散漫，攝之爲難。此篇以元聲元氣立言，可謂知本之論。
同考試官教諭沈批：慨慕古樂，若見其盛，其高志之士歟！
同考試官教諭顏批：樂理極玄，學者罕喻。子論斷古今，多出所見，蓋留心久矣。孰謂天下無鍾期乎？
考試官教諭尹批：知心有元聲元氣，可與言樂矣。
考試官教授薛批：史遷知制律之本，子知作樂之本。
translation_en:
…all followed this path. How much more could be achieved by applying the resources of all under Heaven to it! Could its accomplishments be called merely a minor benefit? Thus I insist that we must begin by valuing grain and conclude by strengthening the agricultural officials’ authority. Only then will the ancient sage kings’ way of allowing the people to recuperate and flourish appear again today. The Spring and Autumn Annals does not record failures of other grain crops, but records failures of millet and wheat, because it places weight on the people’s livelihood. I hope that you, sir, will not consider this impractical.
Third Policy Question
Lin Yixin
Comment by Associate Examiner Hong, Instructor: Creating music depends on nurturing supreme harmony; otherwise, the true essence becomes dispersed and is difficult to gather together. This essay bases its argument on primordial sound and primordial vital energy: it may indeed be called a discourse that understands the root.
Comment by Associate Examiner Shen, Instructor: He ardently admires ancient music, as though beholding its splendor. Surely he is a man of lofty aspirations!
Comment by Associate Examiner Yan, Instructor: The principles of music are profoundly abstruse, and few students understand them. Your judgments concerning past and present frequently arise from your own insights; evidently you have devoted attention to this for a long time. Who says that the world has no Zhong Qi, the discerning listener?
Comment by Examiner Yin, Instructor: Knowing that the heart possesses primordial sound and primordial vital energy, you are someone with whom one can discuss music.
Comment by Examiner Xue, Professor: The historian Sima Qian understood the foundation of establishing pitch standards; you understand the foundation of creating music.

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
先王作樂崇德宣音平化以調天地陰陽
之氣以和神人上下之情故其詩曰鐘鼓
喤喤磬筦鏘鏘降福穰穰其書曰擊石拊
石百獸率舞鳳皇來儀是知樂者天地之
元聲也此聲得則樂可作此樂作則天地
順應鬼神順感萬物咸若天下咸寧而其
遺響餘風雖經千年而不絕故孔子在齊
聞韶而吳札在魯觀舞韶籥者蓋唐虞之
際天地純和而從容禪受不假話言和亦
===
至矣此其作樂之時所以精靈透液妙不
可解有以獨盛而不泯歟是知和者天地
之元氣也元聲元氣相應相含而作樂有
不成者吾未之聞也故夏非不大也承帝
而已矣濩非不雅也救民而已矣武非不
美也定天下而已矣欲其聲容極和美善
兼盡四靈至而百獸舞視韶不有間邪堯
之大章於斯爲盛天機不張而五官皆備
非黃帝咸池之樂張之於洞庭之野者不
punctuated: 先王作樂，崇德宣音，平化，以調天地陰陽之氣，以和神人上下之情。故其詩曰：「鐘鼓喤喤，磬筦鏘鏘，降福穰穰。」其書曰：「擊石拊石，百獸率舞，鳳皇來儀。」是知樂者，天地之元聲也。此聲得，則樂可作；此樂作，則天地順應，鬼神順感，萬物咸若，天下咸寧。而其遺響餘風，雖經千年而不絕。故孔子在齊聞韶，而吳札在魯觀舞韶籥者，蓋唐虞之際，天地純和，而從容禪受，不假話言，和亦至矣。此其作樂之時，所以精靈透液，妙不可解，有以獨盛而不泯歟？是知和者，天地之元氣也。元聲元氣，相應相含，而作樂有不成者，吾未之聞也。故夏非不大也，承帝而已矣；濩非不雅也，救民而已矣；武非不美也，定天下而已矣。欲其聲容極和，美善兼盡，四靈至而百獸舞，視韶不有間邪？堯之大章，於斯爲盛，天機不張而五官皆備，非黃帝咸池之樂張之於洞庭之野者不
translation_en: The former kings created music to exalt virtue, give expression to sound, and bring their transforming influence into balance, thereby attuning the yin and yang energies of Heaven and Earth and harmonizing the feelings of spirits and humans, those above and those below. Thus the Book of Odes says: “Bells and drums resound; stone chimes and pipes ring out; blessings descend in abundance.” The Book of Documents says: “Strike the stones, tap the stones; the hundred beasts all dance, and the phoenix comes in stately bearing.” From this we know that music is the primordial sound of Heaven and Earth. Once this sound is attained, music can be created; once this music is created, Heaven and Earth respond harmoniously, ghosts and spirits are moved in accord, all things flourish, and all under Heaven enjoy peace. Its lingering resonance and surviving influence endure undiminished even after a thousand years. Thus Confucius heard the Shao music in Qi, and Zha of Wu watched the Shao flute dance in Lu. For in the age of Tang Yao and Yu Shun, Heaven and Earth were in perfect harmony, and the throne was yielded and accepted with unhurried ease, without recourse to words. Harmony had indeed reached its utmost. Was this why, when their music was created, its numinous essence permeated and flowed [?], wondrous beyond explanation, enabling it to flourish uniquely and never disappear? From this we know that harmony is the primordial vital energy of Heaven and Earth. When primordial sound and primordial vital energy respond to and contain one another, I have never heard of music being created without success. Thus the Xia music was certainly grand, but it did no more than carry on the work of the sovereign; the Huo music was certainly elegant, but it did no more than save the people; the Wu music was certainly beautiful, but it did no more than pacify all under Heaven. Yet if one demands that their sound and dance attain perfect harmony, fully realizing both beauty and goodness, so that the four numinous creatures arrive and the hundred beasts dance, do they not fall short of the Shao? Yao’s Dazhang, or Great Splendor, excelled in this respect: the workings of nature were unstrained, yet all five faculties were fully provided for. Nothing short of the Yellow Emperor’s Xianchi, or Salty Pool, music, performed in the wilds of Dongting, would …

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
足以倫之也由是推之則羲皇之扶來以
立本神農之扶持以下謀者雖曰遐邈莫
聞然循其義而想像之則冲淡淳龐之趣
幽玄希闊之音宛然若有所見泠然若有
所聞者其視三代已後之樂則不勝節奏
之多聲容之擾矣何足觀哉雖然亦有可
論者也漢興之初高帝不事詩書固難以
語此孝文繼世恭默化民無所改作而馬
遷叙律書推本作樂之意乃首載帝之謝
却將軍陳武用兵之言而且稱嘆天下殷
富百姓和樂意惟此時可以作樂而帝終
始謙讓不肯輕任斯則遷之獨見蓋自班
固以下罕有能識者矣嗣是而景而武嚴
刻奢靡漢之和氣蕩散殆盡雖欲強作其
可得乎故河間獻王雖獻雅樂不過采綴
古事既非一代新制而又止備數歲時不
登宗廟豈非掖庭材人上林樂府內外蠱
惑者眾歟至於哀帝尊尚雅音放絕鄭衛
punctuated: 足以倫之也。由是推之，則羲皇之扶來以立本，神農之扶持以下謀者，雖曰遐邈莫聞，然循其義而想像之，則冲淡淳龐之趣，幽玄希闊之音，宛然若有所見，泠然若有所聞者。其視三代已後之樂，則不勝節奏之多、聲容之擾矣，何足觀哉！雖然，亦有可論者也。漢興之初，高帝不事詩書，固難以語此。孝文繼世，恭默化民，無所改作。而馬遷叙《律書》，推本作樂之意，乃首載帝之謝却將軍陳武用兵之言，而且稱嘆天下殷富，百姓和樂。意惟此時可以作樂，而帝終始謙讓，不肯輕任。斯則遷之獨見，蓋自班固以下，罕有能識者矣。嗣是而景而武，嚴刻奢靡，漢之和氣蕩散殆盡，雖欲強作，其可得乎？故河間獻王雖獻雅樂，不過采綴古事，既非一代新制，而又止備數歲時，不登宗廟，豈非掖庭材人、上林樂府內外蠱惑者眾歟？至於哀帝尊尚雅音，放絕鄭衛，
translation_en:
…could match it. Extending this reasoning, Sovereign Xi’s Coming to Aid (Fulai), which established the foundation, and Shennong’s Sustaining Support (Fuchi), which planned for those below [?], are said to be so remote that nothing of them can be heard. Yet, following their meaning and imagining them, we seem distinctly to perceive their tranquil, simple, and generous spirit, and clearly to hear their profound, mysterious, and rarefied sounds. Compared with these, the music after the Three Dynasties has an unbearable profusion of rhythms and a distracting bustle of sounds and movements. What is there worth observing!

Even so, there is something further to discuss. At the beginning of the Han, Emperor Gao did not devote himself to the Odes and Documents, so it would certainly have been difficult to discuss this with him. Emperor Xiaowen succeeded to the throne and transformed the people through reverence and quietude, making no innovations. Yet when Sima Qian composed the Treatise on the Pitch Pipes and traced the fundamental intention behind making music, he began by recording the emperor’s rejection of General Chen Wu’s proposal to employ military force. He also praised the prosperity of the realm and the harmony and happiness of the people. His implication was that precisely this was a time when music could have been instituted; yet the emperor remained modest and deferential throughout, unwilling to undertake it lightly. This was Qian’s distinctive insight, one that few from Ban Gu onward have been able to recognize.

Thereafter came Emperors Jing and Wu, with harsh severity and extravagant luxury, until the harmonious vital force of the Han had almost entirely dissipated. Even had they wished to force the creation of music, could they have succeeded? Thus, although Prince Xian of Hejian presented elegant ritual music, it merely collected and pieced together ancient practices. It was no new institution for the dynasty, and served only to fill out the complement of performances at seasonal observances, without entering the ancestral temples. Was this not because so many beguiled and corrupted the court, both within and without—the talented women of the Palace Service and the Music Bureau at Shanglin? As for Emperor Ai, he honored elegant music and banished the music of Zheng and Wei…

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
而運祚寢衰卒致新莽攝篡之禍乃其君
德不振威福下移所致非用樂之罪也大
抵聲音之道內與心通外與政通苟得其
道則惟皇建極百官式序國之利器吾得
而執之臣而無有作威作福者矣何下移
之有否則雖朝奏雲門夕鳴韶濩未見其
消姦而化宄也故必達用樂之機者而後
可以爲治端建極之本者而後可以作樂
噫亦大哉此則漢事然矣唐之太宗明皇
===
號稱英辟故皆收錄雅樂斟酌裁定被之
管絃其志有足稱者而胡部俗樂如巴渝
西凉之曲霓裳羽衣之舞眩目奪聰雜然
竝進不知二君何以閑情也魏文侯聆古
樂而恐臥晉文公聞新聲而忘食者將非
是乎故漁陽鼙鼓感召而來非一朝一夕
之故也是其樂雖謂之胡可也雅何有哉
此則唐事然矣宋至天聖景祐之間承平
日久天下晏然故仁宗留意禮樂之事而
punctuated:
而運祚寢衰，卒致新莽攝篡之禍，乃其君德不振、威福下移所致，非用樂之罪也。大抵聲音之道，內與心通，外與政通。苟得其道，則惟皇建極，百官式序，國之利器吾得而執之，臣而無有作威作福者矣，何下移之有？否則，雖朝奏雲門，夕鳴韶濩，未見其消姦而化宄也。故必達用樂之機者，而後可以爲治；端建極之本者，而後可以作樂。噫，亦大哉！此則漢事然矣。
唐之太宗、明皇，號稱英辟，故皆收錄雅樂，斟酌裁定，被之管絃，其志有足稱者。而胡部俗樂，如巴渝、西凉之曲，霓裳羽衣之舞，眩目奪聰，雜然竝進，不知二君何以閑情也？魏文侯聆古樂而恐臥，晉文公聞新聲而忘食者，將非是乎？故漁陽鼙鼓，感召而來，非一朝一夕之故也。是其樂雖謂之胡可也，雅何有哉？此則唐事然矣。
宋至天聖、景祐之間，承平日久，天下晏然，故仁宗留意禮樂之事，而
translation_en:
…yet the dynasty’s fortunes gradually declined, ultimately bringing the calamity of Wang Mang’s assumption of the regency and usurpation to establish Xin. This resulted from the ruler’s failure to strengthen his virtue and from the transfer of authority to punish and reward into subordinate hands; it was not the fault of employing music. In general, the way of musical sounds communicates inwardly with the heart and outwardly with government. If its proper way is attained, the sovereign establishes the supreme standard, the hundred officials take their proper places, and the potent instruments of the state remain in the ruler’s grasp. No minister then arrogates the power to punish or reward. How could authority pass into subordinate hands? Otherwise, even if “Cloud Gate” were performed in the morning and the Shao and Huo music sounded in the evening, we would not see them eliminate treachery or reform evildoers. Thus only one who understands the crucial workings of music’s use can govern, and only one who sets right the foundation for establishing the supreme standard can institute music. Ah, how momentous this is! Such was the case under the Han.
Tang Taizong and Minghuang were reputed to be enlightened sovereigns. Both therefore collected court ritual music, deliberated over and revised it, and arranged it for wind and string instruments. Their intentions deserve praise. Yet popular music from the foreign ensembles, such as the tunes of Ba-Yu and Xiliang and the dance “Rainbow Skirts and Feathered Robes,” dazzled the eyes and overwhelmed the hearing, all being presented together. I do not know how these two rulers could thereby have kept their passions in check. Was this not like Marquis Wen of Wei fearing that he would fall asleep when listening to ancient music, and Duke Wen of Jin [?] forgetting to eat when hearing new sounds? Thus the war drums of Yuyang came in response to what had called them forth; their causes did not arise in a single morning or evening. Their music might indeed be called foreign, but what was ritual music about it? Such was the case under the Tang.
By the Tiansheng and Jingyou eras of the Song, peace had long prevailed, and all under Heaven was tranquil. Renzong therefore devoted attention to matters of ritual and music, and…

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
太常燕肅謂金石不調請求考正後雖更
制竟無成績及政和之時國事廢壞樂之
泣聲應之而君臣不務脩德但圖造樂且
多大晟之成喜動顏色豈知女眞之禍將
至而乖戾不諧之音先見於金石絲竹之
內也師曠識紂樂於濮水萬寶常泫隋禍
於江都不類是乎故其樂雖謂之不作可
也其何益哉若或享國靈長或遘害酷烈
乃其創業天命之定守成人事之變固非
===
樂之制與不制之應也大抵上古之樂有
意無聲故其神藏隆古之樂有聲無文故
其機隱三代之樂聲文極備故其懿著漢
唐已來皆剽竊文具聊備一代之典章而
已樂云乎哉獨漢文之時其會可乘而帝
則自失遂使玄音妙理千有餘年而不流
聞於世不亦深可惜乎雖然吾心有元聲
焉吾心有元氣焉以吾之聲合樂之聲以
吾之氣合樂之氣則陰陽運而律呂調金
punctuated:
太常燕肅謂金石不調，請求考正，後雖更制，竟無成績。及政和之時，國事廢壞，樂之泣聲應之，而君臣不務脩德，但圖造樂，且多大晟之成，喜動顏色，豈知女眞之禍將至，而乖戾不諧之音先見於金石絲竹之內也？師曠識紂樂於濮水，萬寶常泫隋禍於江都，不類是乎？故其樂雖謂之不作可也，其何益哉？若或享國靈長，或遘害酷烈，乃其創業天命之定、守成人事之變，固非樂之制與不制之應也。
大抵上古之樂，有意無聲，故其神藏；隆古之樂，有聲無文，故其機隱；三代之樂，聲文極備，故其懿著。漢唐已來，皆剽竊文具，聊備一代之典章而已，樂云乎哉？獨漢文之時，其會可乘，而帝則自失，遂使玄音妙理千有餘年而不流聞於世，不亦深可惜乎？
雖然，吾心有元聲焉，吾心有元氣焉。以吾之聲合樂之聲，以吾之氣合樂之氣，則陰陽運而律呂調，金
translation_en:
…Yan Su, an official of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, said that the bells and chime stones were out of tune and requested that they be examined and corrected. Although the musical system was subsequently revised, nothing was ultimately accomplished. By the Zhenghe era, affairs of state had fallen into ruin, and the weeping tones of the music responded accordingly. Yet ruler and ministers devoted themselves neither to cultivating virtue nor to its practice, but only to making music. They even praised the completion of the Dasheng music, delight showing on their faces. How could they have known that disaster at the hands of the Jurchens was approaching, and that discordant, inharmonious sounds had already appeared in their bells, chime stones, strings, and pipes? Shi Kuang recognized the music of Zhou, the last Shang king, at the Pu River; Wan Baochang shed tears over the disaster that would befall the Sui at Jiangdu. Were these not similar cases? Thus one might as well say that their music had never been made: what benefit did it bring? Whether a dynasty enjoyed a long reign or encountered devastating calamity depended on Heaven’s mandate as fixed at its founding and on changes in human affairs as its successors maintained the inheritance. These outcomes were certainly not responses to whether music had or had not been instituted.
Generally speaking, the music of earliest antiquity had intent but no sound, so its spiritual power remained concealed. The music of high antiquity had sound but no patterned elaboration, so its workings remained hidden. In the Three Dynasties, sound and patterned elaboration were fully developed, so the excellence of music became manifest. From the Han and Tang onward, all merely borrowed outward forms, furnishing the institutions of a dynasty and nothing more. Could this be called music? Only in the time of Emperor Wen of Han was there an opportunity that could have been seized, but the emperor himself let it slip. Consequently, for more than a thousand years, the profound tones and subtle principles of music have not circulated and been heard in the world. Is this not deeply regrettable?
Nevertheless, within my heart there is primordial sound; within my heart there is primordial vital energy. If I bring my sound into harmony with the sound of music, and my vital energy into harmony with the vital energy of music, then yin and yang will circulate and the pitch standards will be attuned, and the bells…

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
石協而節奏順矣然豈易能乎必聖人在
天子之位建中和之極反純朴之眞使萬
事盡理萬物盡育四夷盡賓而太和之氣
充塞兩間包表四極然後陰陽會精鬼神
效靈大樂有成天地和同王道備而治化
極矣方今
聖天子在上懋德建中治隆化洽尊崇
宗廟順正郊壇訓典儀章煥然星列雖放勳重
華之盛無以加矣顧太常樂部尚襲舊物
===
不亦昭代之闕典乎請自今伊始於禮官
之屬專設一署而以儒臣之審音者掌之
博選其人優之員秩使之循習器數歌舞
聲容假以歲年俟其自得如此則必有師
曠州鳩之神解妙悟者出以鳴我
聖天子中和位育之盛韶濩可追而漢唐宋在
所不言也愚生何幸將躬親見之哉
第四問
鄭逑
punctuated:
石協而節奏順矣。然豈易能乎？必聖人在天子之位，建中和之極，反純朴之眞，使萬事盡理，萬物盡育，四夷盡賓，而太和之氣充塞兩間，包表四極，然後陰陽會精，鬼神效靈，大樂有成，天地和同，王道備而治化極矣。方今聖天子在上，懋德建中，治隆化洽，尊崇宗廟，順正郊壇，訓典儀章，煥然星列。雖放勳重華之盛，無以加矣。顧太常樂部尚襲舊物，不亦昭代之闕典乎？請自今伊始，於禮官之屬專設一署，而以儒臣之審音者掌之，博選其人，優之員秩，使之循習器數、歌舞、聲容，假以歲年，俟其自得。如此，則必有師曠州鳩之神解妙悟者出，以鳴我聖天子中和位育之盛，韶濩可追，而漢唐宋在所不言也。愚生何幸，將躬親見之哉！
第四問
鄭逑
translation_en:
…the stone chimes sound in concord, and the rhythms proceed smoothly. Yet how could this be easily accomplished? A sage must occupy the position of Son of Heaven, establish the supreme standard of equilibrium and harmony, and restore the authenticity of unadorned simplicity, so that all affairs are properly ordered, all things fully nurtured, and the peoples of the four quarters all submit. The vital force of supreme harmony must fill the space between Heaven and Earth and extend beyond the four extremities. Only then will yin and yang unite their essences and the spirits manifest their efficacy. Great music will attain perfection, Heaven and Earth will harmonize, the Kingly Way will be complete, and governance and moral transformation will reach their utmost heights.
At present, our sage Son of Heaven reigns above, cultivating virtue and establishing equilibrium. His governance flourishes and his transforming influence reaches everywhere. He reveres the ancestral temples and duly orders the suburban sacrificial altars; canonical instructions and ceremonial regulations shine like an array of stars. Even the flourishing ages of Fangxun and Chonghua—Yao and Shun—could not surpass this. Yet the music department of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices still retains its old equipment. Is this not a deficiency in the institutions of our illustrious age?
I request that, beginning now, a dedicated office be established under the ritual officials, with Confucian officials versed in musical tones placed in charge. Its personnel should be broadly recruited and generously provided with posts and ranks. Let them practice the prescribed use of instruments, song and dance, and musical and choreographic forms; allow them years to achieve understanding for themselves. In this way, men possessing the inspired understanding and subtle insight of Shi Kuang and Zhou Jiu will surely emerge to give musical expression to the flourishing equilibrium and harmony under our sage Son of Heaven, whereby Heaven and Earth take their proper places and all things are nurtured. The Shao and Huo music of antiquity could then be emulated, while the music of the Han, Tang, and Song would scarcely merit mention. How fortunate I, this humble student, would be to witness it in person!
Fourth Question
Zheng Qiu

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭吳批六經殘缺無可奈何而
世儒率欲附會如近代偽作三墳亦稱古書殊非博雅矧
聖人精蘊不在言語文字之閒存者尚多何憂喪失此篇
頗有曠達之識是用錄出
同考試官教諭甘批在昔盛時天子同文故
雖孔子作經惟稱竊比不敢自任自秦火後因購遺書遂
開妄作之隙多書之害至今未息有識之士私常患之不
意舉業之士能知言至此
考試官教諭尹批觀歷代藏書多所亡失
===
乃知作者雖多傳者不幾錄子此篇用為多士
之戒
考試官教授薛批經之殘者不必補綴故
今文古文六典二戴等書學者至今疑之昔人有言遺經
抱終始子是之見蓋亦有同云
夫書契既作文籍肇生伏羲堯舜文王周
公相繼數千年閒羣書始備歷世寶之無
敢加焉迨春秋之世明王不興聖人未出
而三墳五典八索九丘諸書蕪穢龐雜托
punctuated:
同考試官教諭吳批：六經殘缺，無可奈何，而世儒率欲附會，如近代偽作三墳，亦稱古書，殊非博雅。矧聖人精蘊不在言語文字之閒，存者尚多，何憂喪失？此篇頗有曠達之識，是用錄出。

同考試官教諭甘批：在昔盛時，天子同文，故雖孔子作經，惟稱竊比，不敢自任。自秦火後，因購遺書，遂開妄作之隙。多書之害，至今未息，有識之士私常患之。不意舉業之士能知言至此。

考試官教諭尹批：觀歷代藏書，多所亡失，乃知作者雖多，傳者不幾。錄子此篇，用為多士之戒。

考試官教授薛批：經之殘者，不必補綴，故今文、古文、六典、二戴等書，學者至今疑之。昔人有言：「遺經抱終始。」子是之見，蓋亦有同云。

夫書契既作，文籍肇生，伏羲、堯、舜、文王、周公，相繼數千年閒，羣書始備。歷世寶之，無敢加焉。迨春秋之世，明王不興，聖人未出，而三墳、五典、八索、九丘諸書，蕪穢龐雜，托
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor: The Six Classics are incomplete, and nothing can be done about it. Yet scholars commonly seek to force connections, as with the recently fabricated Three Ancient Records (San fen), which they also call an ancient book. This is hardly sound and extensive learning. Moreover, the sages’ profound teachings do not reside in words and writing alone. Much still survives: why worry about what has been lost? This essay shows considerable breadth of understanding, and for this reason it has been selected for inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Gan, Instructor: In the flourishing ages of antiquity, the Son of Heaven unified writing. Thus even Confucius, when composing the classics, spoke only of “presuming to compare” himself with earlier worthies and did not dare claim such authority for himself. After the Qin burning of books, the purchase of surviving writings opened the way to fabrications. The harm caused by this proliferation of books has not ceased to this day, and discerning men have often privately lamented it. I did not expect a student preparing for the examinations to attain such discernment in judging writings.

Comment by Examiner Yin, Instructor: Looking at the books collected over successive dynasties, we find that many have been lost. We thus realize that although authors have been numerous, few of their works have survived. I include this essay of yours as a warning to the many students.

Comment by Examiner Xue, Professor: There is no need to patch together the incomplete classics. Thus scholars to this day remain doubtful about such texts as the New Text and Old Text versions, the Six Canons (Liu dian), and the works of the two Dai. Someone of old said, “The surviving classics embrace beginning and end.” Your view here seems to accord with this.

Once written signs were devised, written records first came into being. Fuxi, Yao, Shun, King Wen, and the Duke of Zhou succeeded one another over several thousand years before the body of writings was complete. Successive ages treasured them, and no one dared add to them. By the Spring and Autumn period, no enlightened king had arisen and the sage had not yet appeared. Such books as the Three Ancient Records (San fen), Five Canons (Wu dian), Eight Cords (Ba suo), and Nine Mounds (Jiu qiu) were corrupt and confused, sprawling and miscellaneous, and falsely attributed …

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
名上古楚左史倚相讀之貴之曰能孔子
出而一切憂之讚易以黜誕定禮樂以黜
僭刪詩書以黜不雅脩春秋以黜不王然
後六經之道如日中天萬目利覩而倚相
所讀者遂亡聖作而異端伏經成而羣書
散也及其沒也邪說巫風盈滿天下雖以
子思孟軻之賢尚口窮辯脩辭力詆竟莫
能止曾幾何年遂罹秦火之害然後知六
經之全缺關世運之隆汙羣書之存亡視
===
六經之顯晦也故易詩春秋苟無見焉雖
全無益也尚書三禮苟有見焉雖缺何損
也若不持此求書而惟全缺之視則五官
已繁雖足冬官而何用古文雖出豈盡虞
夏商周之舊哉故醫卜種樹之不存猶燔
燎毁棄之不亡者也故必明王在上聖人
佐之口代天言身代天事神而明之從一
陶鑄庶乎六經爲完書也不然搜購雖廣
綴葺雖全不過孔壁汲冢之餘耳豈能得
punctuated: 名上古。楚左史倚相讀之，貴之曰能。孔子出而一切憂之，讚易以黜誕，定禮樂以黜僭，刪詩書以黜不雅，脩春秋以黜不王。然後六經之道如日中天，萬目利覩，而倚相所讀者遂亡。聖作而異端伏，經成而羣書散也。及其沒也，邪說巫風盈滿天下，雖以子思孟軻之賢，尚口窮辯、脩辭力詆，竟莫能止。曾幾何年，遂罹秦火之害。然後知六經之全缺，關世運之隆汙；羣書之存亡，視六經之顯晦也。故易、詩、春秋苟無見焉，雖全無益也；尚書、三禮苟有見焉，雖缺何損也？若不持此求書，而惟全缺之視，則五官已繁，雖足冬官而何用？古文雖出，豈盡虞夏商周之舊哉？故醫卜種樹之不存，猶燔燎毁棄之不亡者也。故必明王在上，聖人佐之，口代天言，身代天事，神而明之，從一陶鑄，庶乎六經爲完書也。不然，搜購雖廣，綴葺雖全，不過孔壁汲冢之餘耳，豈能得
translation_en:
…claiming the authority of high antiquity. Yixiang, the Scribe of the Left of Chu, read these works and was esteemed as an able man for doing so. When Confucius appeared, he was troubled by all of this. He elucidated the Changes to reject the fantastic, established the rites and music to reject usurpation, edited the Odes and Documents to reject what was improper, and revised the Spring and Autumn Annals to reject departures from true kingship. Only then did the Way of the Six Classics shine like the sun at midday, plainly visible to all eyes, while the works Yixiang had read subsequently disappeared. When the sage arose, heterodox teachings were subdued; when the Classics were established, the other writings dispersed. After his death, pernicious doctrines and shamanistic practices filled the world. Even men as worthy as Zisi and Meng Ke exhausted their powers of oral argument and marshalled their words in vigorous refutation, yet ultimately could not stop them. Before many years had passed, the Classics suffered the calamity of the Qin book burning. Only then can we understand that the completeness or incompleteness of the Six Classics is bound up with the flourishing or decline of the age, and that the survival or disappearance of other writings depends on whether the Six Classics are manifest or obscured.

Thus, if one gains no insight from the Changes, Odes, and Spring and Autumn Annals, their completeness is of no benefit. If one gains insight from the Book of Documents and the Three Ritual Classics, what harm does their incompleteness do? If one seeks texts without holding to this principle and attends only to their completeness or incompleteness, the five offices are already amply treated: what use would completing the Offices of Winter serve? Even if the Old Text Documents were to appear, could they contain all the original writings of Yu, Xia, Shang, and Zhou? Thus, the failure of writings on medicine, divination, and tree cultivation to survive is like the failure of writings burned and discarded to perish [?]. There must therefore be an enlightened king above, assisted by a sage, speaking on Heaven’s behalf and acting in Heaven’s stead, bringing spiritual insight to bear and fashioning everything according to a single principle. Only then might the Six Classics become complete books. Otherwise, however widely texts are sought and purchased, and however fully their fragments are pieced together, they amount to no more than remnants from the wall of Confucius’s house and the tomb at Ji. How could one obtain…

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
其眞乎秦火旣息漢氏代立挾書之令罷
獻書之路開誠世道轉移之一機也奈何
陋儒藉是希寵剽竊舊義曲加潤色甚則
僞作而私傳之以要爵賞於是稽古雖榮
而經道復晦矣故書不再火而識者已知
其有可亡之漸下逮隋人爰至唐宋非無
蘭臺石室之藏寶軸錦標之異集賢麗正
之所太平淳化之號然世代一移輒成灰
燼奚待稽之藝文假之書數然後知其所
===
亡者乎獨宋之王堯臣所撰崇文總目百
家小說無一不備君子已非其非館閣藏
書之體而或者更謂尚有缺略不亦好奇
之過乎蓋茫唐淺陋世自有不傳之書逸
放沉淪書亦多不幸之變而載籍之繁文
詞之盛則固政治之妨忠信之薄也與其
無益而存曷若不幸而亡乎故必明王在
上賢人輔之同文軌物不使無知妄作庶
於六經不背而且不晦也不然則兎盡中
punctuated: 其眞乎？秦火旣息，漢氏代立，挾書之令罷，獻書之路開，誠世道轉移之一機也。奈何陋儒藉是希寵，剽竊舊義，曲加潤色，甚則僞作而私傳之，以要爵賞。於是稽古雖榮，而經道復晦矣。故書不再火，而識者已知其有可亡之漸。下逮隋人，爰至唐宋，非無蘭臺石室之藏、寶軸錦標之異、集賢麗正之所、太平淳化之號，然世代一移，輒成灰燼。奚待稽之藝文，假之書數，然後知其所亡者乎？獨宋之王堯臣所撰《崇文總目》，百家小說，無一不備。君子已非其非館閣藏書之體，而或者更謂尚有缺略，不亦好奇之過乎？蓋茫唐淺陋，世自有不傳之書；逸放沉淪，書亦多不幸之變。而載籍之繁、文詞之盛，則固政治之妨、忠信之薄也。與其無益而存，曷若不幸而亡乎？故必明王在上，賢人輔之，同文軌物，不使無知妄作，庶於六經不背而且不晦也。不然，則兎盡中
translation_en:
…their true substance? Once the fires of Qin had died out and the Han house had succeeded to power, the prohibition on possessing books was abolished and channels for presenting books were opened. This was indeed an opportunity to change the course of the age. Yet shallow scholars exploited it to seek favor: they plagiarized old interpretations and elaborately embellished them; some even fabricated works and circulated them privately to obtain ranks and rewards. Thus, although the study of antiquity enjoyed honor, the Way of the Classics was again obscured. Even without another burning of books, discerning people already recognized the beginnings of their possible destruction. From the Sui down through the Tang and Song, there was no lack of collections in the Orchid Terrace and Stone Chamber, magnificent scrolls with precious rollers and brocade labels, institutions such as Jixian and Lizheng, or compilations bearing the names Taiping and Chunhua. Yet whenever a dynasty changed, these were reduced to ashes. Why need one wait to examine bibliographical records and consult book counts [?] before knowing what had been lost?

Consider Wang Yaochen of the Song and his General Catalogue for the Veneration of Literature (Chongwen zongmu): it included every sort of miscellaneous anecdotal writing from the various schools, omitting nothing. Gentlemen already criticized it for failing to conform to the proper standards of an imperial library collection, yet some went further and claimed that it still had omissions. Was this not an excessive appetite for curiosities? Rambling and shallow works naturally include books that the world does not transmit; books also suffer many unfortunate vicissitudes, becoming scattered or sinking into oblivion. Yet the proliferation of writings and the profusion of literary compositions certainly impede government and weaken loyalty and trustworthiness. Rather than survive without benefit, would they not better be lost through misfortune?

There must therefore be an enlightened king above, assisted by worthy men, who unifies writing and regulates affairs, preventing the ignorant from producing reckless compositions. Only then might writings neither depart from the Six Classics nor obscure them. Otherwise, even if all the rabbits were used up in Zhong…

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
山竹盡南國不足以供毛楮之用而毌剥
相尋窮上反下其勢不至於燔燎殆盡不
止也其誰能拯之乎然世之君子往往愛
尚纂集括爲成書如劉歆之七略荀勗之
四部王儉之七志阮孝緒之七録者何可
勝數而晁公武則就南陽所藏總之爲讀
書記陳振孫則就家塾所有名之爲書録
解題管轄百家筌蹄六籍其心苦以專其
力勞而久可謂博雅君子矣然卽其書而
===
觀之廣采詳論雖大學之一端而寡要曠
功終儒者之末事矣究其本末察其眞僞
權其純駁其亦王應麟馬端臨之儔歟而
馬端臨則又竊取三人之所論次者入之
文獻通考不亦掠人之甚乎大抵萃類之
書皆剪芟經傳决裂義理使人利於誦覽
不求全文實亡書之媒殘經之寳也故必
明王在上儒臣主之擇定見書數種布式
天下著在法典有不遵者加之常刑如此
punctuated: 山，竹盡南國，不足以供毛楮之用，而毌剥相尋，窮上反下，其勢不至於燔燎殆盡不止也。其誰能拯之乎？然世之君子往往愛尚纂集，括爲成書，如劉歆之《七略》、荀勗之《四部》、王儉之《七志》、阮孝緒之《七録》者，何可勝數？而晁公武則就南陽所藏，總之爲《讀書記》；陳振孫則就家塾所有，名之爲《書録解題》。管轄百家，筌蹄六籍，其心苦以專，其力勞而久，可謂博雅君子矣。然卽其書而觀之，廣采詳論，雖大學之一端，而寡要曠功，終儒者之末事矣。究其本末，察其眞僞，權其純駁，其亦王應麟、馬端臨之儔歟？而馬端臨則又竊取三人之所論次者，入之《文獻通考》，不亦掠人之甚乎？大抵萃類之書，皆剪芟經傳，决裂義理，使人利於誦覽，不求全文，實亡書之媒、殘經之寳也。故必明王在上，儒臣主之，擇定見書數種，布式天下，著在法典，有不遵者，加之常刑。如此，
translation_en:
…shan, and even if all the bamboo in the southern lands were exhausted, these would not suffice to supply the brushes and paper required. Destruction and stripping would follow one another [?], exhausting what is above and turning upon what is below; this tendency would not stop until almost everything had been burned away. Who could rescue the situation?

Yet gentlemen of the world often delight in compiling collections and gathering them into books. Works such as Liu Xin’s Seven Summaries, Xun Xu’s Four Divisions, Wang Jian’s Seven Treatises, and Ruan Xiaoxu’s Seven Records are too numerous to count. Chao Gongwu brought together descriptions of the holdings at Nanyang to make his Record of Reading; Chen Zhensun drew upon the holdings of his family school and entitled his work Explanatory Notices to a Catalogue of Books. Encompassing the hundred schools and providing tools for grasping the Six Classics, they applied their minds painstakingly and single-mindedly, and labored long and hard. They may indeed be called gentlemen of broad learning and refined scholarship.

Yet when one examines their books, extensive collection and detailed discussion, though one aspect of great learning, yield little of essential importance at great expenditure of effort. They remain, ultimately, secondary pursuits for a Confucian scholar. In investigating origins and ramifications, distinguishing the genuine from the spurious, and weighing the pure against the mixed, were they perhaps peers of Wang Yinglin and Ma Duanlin? Yet Ma Duanlin in turn appropriated what three men had discussed and arranged, incorporating it into his Comprehensive Examination of Documents and Institutions. Was this not an extreme instance of plundering others?

In general, books that gather material by category all cut and prune the classics and their commentaries and tear apart their principles. They encourage readers to take advantage of convenient recitation and perusal without seeking the complete texts. They are truly agents of the loss of books and treasures for mutilating the classics. Thus there must be an enlightened king above, with Confucian ministers directing the undertaking, selecting and approving several kinds of extant books, promulgating a standard throughout the realm, and incorporating it into the statutory code. Those who fail to comply should receive the prescribed punishments. In this way …

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
則人讀全書學致全力六經之域可踐而
聖人之蘊可窺矣不然則終年叅校累歲
編摩祗亦古人之糟粕耳其何有於我乎
故嘗爲之言曰人不力學以書之多人不
脩行以文之盛國不善治以人之浮然則
必何如而後可中庸曰非天子不議禮不
制度不考文孟子曰經正則庶民興庶民
興斯無邪慝矣狂陋之見如此不知執事
以爲何如
===
第五問
徐梹
同考試官教諭曾 批 養兵之費人人知之而
不能言言之而不能施此作謂宜歸之於農而不泥古人
之迹又不引唐兵爲證深識遠慮措而行之富强可不外
此而致矣真知言哉
考試官教諭尹 批 亹亹千餘言皆盡事實
非素有志於斯世者不能到錄之以傳庶天下之爲士者
知用心於
punctuated:
則人讀全書，學致全力，六經之域可踐，而聖人之蘊可窺矣。不然，則終年叅校，累歲編摩，祗亦古人之糟粕耳，其何有於我乎？故嘗爲之言曰：「人不力學，以書之多；人不脩行，以文之盛；國不善治，以人之浮。」然則必何如而後可？《中庸》曰：「非天子，不議禮，不制度，不考文。」《孟子》曰：「經正則庶民興，庶民興斯無邪慝矣。」狂陋之見如此，不知執事以爲何如？

第五問
徐梹

同考試官教諭曾批：養兵之費，人人知之，而不能言；言之，而不能施。此作謂宜歸之於農，而不泥古人之迹，又不引唐兵爲證。深識遠慮，措而行之，富强可不外此而致矣。真知言哉！

考試官教諭尹批：亹亹千餘言，皆盡事實，非素有志於斯世者不能到。錄之以傳，庶天下之爲士者知用心於
translation_en:
…then people would read books in their entirety and devote their full efforts to learning; they could enter the realm of the Six Classics and glimpse the profound teachings of the sages. Otherwise, though they spend whole years collating texts and successive years compiling them, these remain merely the dregs of the ancients. What would I myself have gained from them? Thus I once said: “People fail to study diligently because books are so numerous; people fail to cultivate their conduct because literary writing is so abundant; the state fails to achieve good government because people are so superficial.” What, then, must be done to set matters right? The Doctrine of the Mean says: “Unless one is the Son of Heaven, one does not deliberate on ritual, establish institutions and standards, or examine written forms.” The Mencius says: “When the canonical principles are rectified, the common people will rise to goodness; when the common people rise to goodness, there will be no wickedness or depravity.” Such are my rash and ill-informed views. I wonder what you, sir, think of them.

Fifth Question
Xu Bin 徐梹

Comment by Associate Examiner Zeng, Instructor: Everyone knows the expense of maintaining troops, yet cannot explain what to do about it; those who can explain it cannot put their proposals into practice. This essay argues that military support should be rooted in agriculture, without clinging rigidly to ancient precedents. Nor does it cite the Tang military system as evidence. It shows deep understanding and far-reaching foresight. If its proposals were put into effect, wealth and strength could be attained through these measures alone. Truly, these are discerning words!

Comment by Examiner Yin, Instructor: More than a thousand words flow forth, all fully grounded in the facts of affairs. Such a level could be attained only by someone long committed to the concerns of the present age. I record it for circulation, in the hope that scholars throughout the realm will know to devote their attention to…

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
當代之制矣此之謂眞才
考試官敎授薛批才幾賈誼而術不疎
對天下之費固有名重而實輕者不急之
費而被之以莫大之名是以天下常疑之
而不敢動持之而莫敢議何者舉其事則
必有以成其謀倡天下以必勞之事而巳
欲獨處其逸其勢固有所不能而況天下
大計所寓非一旦之力所能必其有成也
苟非一旦之力可成則其間中沮中變意
===
外之隱虞有不可保者嗚呼謀之而未必
行行之而未必終而且有隱虞以伏于吾
之前後則吾亦何爲蹈不測之險任累歲
之勞以圖不可期之功耶噫此養兵之費
所以不聞論列蓋自宋室而巳然矣然當
時人主亦未嘗不以爲意往往形之詔旨
親加校閱而卒不能弘宋祖建隆之規而
卒成慶曆之弊者言人人殊愛其勞而樂
因循也姑舉一二爲執事陳之建隆間命
punctuated:
當代之制矣。此之謂眞才。

考試官敎授薛批：才幾賈誼，而術不疎。

對：天下之費，固有名重而實輕者。不急之費，而被之以莫大之名，是以天下常疑之而不敢動，持之而莫敢議。何者？舉其事，則必有以成其謀。倡天下以必勞之事，而巳欲獨處其逸，其勢固有所不能，而況天下大計所寓，非一旦之力所能必其有成也。苟非一旦之力可成，則其間中沮中變，意外之隱虞，有不可保者。嗚呼！謀之而未必行，行之而未必終，而且有隱虞以伏于吾之前後，則吾亦何爲蹈不測之險，任累歲之勞，以圖不可期之功耶？噫！此養兵之費所以不聞論列，蓋自宋室而巳然矣。然當時人主亦未嘗不以爲意，往往形之詔旨，親加校閱，而卒不能弘宋祖建隆之規，而卒成慶曆之弊者，言人人殊，愛其勞而樂因循也。姑舉一二爲執事陳之。建隆間，命
translation_en:
…the institutions of the present age. This is what may be called true talent.

Examiner Xue, an instructor, comments: His talent approaches that of Jia Yi, yet his methods are not impractical.

Response: Among the expenditures of the realm, there are certainly some whose importance is great in name but slight in substance. Expenditure that is not urgent is invested with a supremely important name. Thus people throughout the realm constantly doubt it yet dare not change it; they maintain it, and none dares debate it. Why is this? To undertake an enterprise, one must have the means to bring the plan to completion. To call upon the realm to undertake something necessarily toilsome while wishing oneself alone to remain at ease [疑: 巳, apparently meaning “oneself”] is inherently impossible. Moreover, where the great plans of the realm are involved, success cannot be assured through a single day’s exertion. If something cannot be accomplished in a single day, then setbacks and changes along the way, together with unforeseen hidden dangers, cannot be guarded against with certainty. Alas! A plan may not be put into practice; once put into practice, it may not be carried through. And when hidden dangers lie in wait before and behind us, why should we venture into unpredictable peril and shoulder years of toil to seek an achievement whose realization cannot be assured?

Ah! This is why we hear no reasoned discussion of the expense of maintaining troops. It has apparently been so since the Song dynasty. Yet the rulers of that time did concern themselves with it. They frequently expressed their concern in edicts and personally inspected the troops. That they ultimately failed to extend the arrangements established by the Song founding emperor in the Jianlong reign, and ultimately produced the abuses of the Qingli reign, was because everyone offered different advice, begrudged the toil, and preferred to follow established practice. Let me set out one or two examples for your consideration. During the Jianlong reign, an order was issued…

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
殿前侍衛諸州守臣各閱所部兵士汰其
耄懦而擇其超然雄勇者升之上軍尋又
下令荆南放逐老兵他兵有願歸農者官
給田屋自是詔免之兵疊見史冊嗚呼宋
祖之意微矣使其後世能推廣之則宋之
為宋未可知也顧代自為制或是或否譬
則一齊衆楚雖有所為終亦無濟何以言
之真宗屢詔内外簡汰士卒矣及令轉運
使閱驗沿邊老兵悉遣歸農矣迨夫神宗
===
又撥併軍營减軍員十將以下三千餘人
一歲省錢四十五萬緡米四十萬石布草
稱是且令轉運使經畫之矣此咸平煕寧
之間所以號稱饒裕而慶曆以來不能率
循其法顧乃務增兵數廣軍額至一百餘
萬此何為者耶夫所貴於兵者以其威戎
狄則能制勝禦盗賊則能止奸非徒張皇
人數也自黄帝蚩尤以來無慮數千戰矣
蓋未聞以人多勝者光武以六千人而敗
punctuated: 殿前、侍衛、諸州守臣各閱所部兵士，汰其耄懦，而擇其超然雄勇者升之上軍。尋又下令荆南放逐老兵，他兵有願歸農者，官給田屋。自是詔免之兵疊見史冊。嗚呼！宋祖之意微矣！使其後世能推廣之，則宋之為宋未可知也。顧代自為制，或是或否，譬則一齊衆楚，雖有所為，終亦無濟。何以言之？真宗屢詔内外簡汰士卒矣，及令轉運使閱驗沿邊老兵，悉遣歸農矣。迨夫神宗，又撥併軍營，减軍員十將以下三千餘人，一歲省錢四十五萬緡、米四十萬石，布草稱是，且令轉運使經畫之矣。此咸平、煕寧之間所以號稱饒裕，而慶曆以來不能率循其法，顧乃務增兵數，廣軍額至一百餘萬，此何為者耶？夫所貴於兵者，以其威戎狄則能制勝，禦盗賊則能止奸，非徒張皇人數也。自黄帝、蚩尤以來，無慮數千戰矣，蓋未聞以人多勝者。光武以六千人而敗
translation_en:
…the Palace Command, the Palace Guard, and the prefectural governors each to review the soldiers under their command, discharge the aged and feeble, and select those of exceptional strength and courage for promotion to the superior army units. Soon afterward, he also ordered Jingnan to dismiss its old soldiers; other soldiers who wished to return to farming were to receive fields and houses from the authorities. Thereafter, discharges of soldiers by imperial decree appear repeatedly in the historical records. Ah! Profound was the intention of the founding emperor of the Song! Had his successors been able to extend this policy, there is no telling what the Song might have become. Yet each reign established its own arrangements, some sound and others unsound. It was like one man speaking the language of Qi amid a crowd speaking that of Chu: whatever he attempted would ultimately be of no avail.

Why do I say this? Emperor Zhenzong repeatedly ordered the screening and dismissal of soldiers both at the capital and in the provinces. He also ordered the transport commissioners to inspect the old soldiers along the frontier and send them all back to farming. Under Emperor Shenzong, military camps were further reorganized and consolidated, and military personnel at the rank of commander of ten and below were reduced by more than three thousand. This saved 450,000 strings of cash and 400,000 shi of grain annually, with proportionate savings in cloth and fodder. He also ordered the transport commissioners to plan and administer these measures. This was why the Xianping and Xining periods enjoyed a reputation for abundance. Yet from the Qingli period onward, they failed to follow these methods, instead striving to increase troop numbers and expand the authorized military establishment to more than a million. What purpose did this serve?

What makes soldiers valuable is their ability to secure victory when overawing the Rong and Di, and to suppress wrongdoing when resisting bandits—not merely to make an imposing display of numbers. Since the time of the Yellow Emperor and Chiyou, there have been thousands of battles, yet we have never heard of victory being secured through numbers alone. Guangwu, with six thousand men, defeated…

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
王尋等百萬之師苻堅百萬之衆不能當
東晉之三萬曹操恃其三十萬衆而敗於
吕布及歸許而悟也遂能以二萬破袁紹
四十萬之衆此兵多必敗兵少則勝之明
驗也彼慶曆君臣計不出此竭天下之財
力浚百姓之膏髓崇虛名以養無用之兵
卒之國勢日以卑弱而海內日以虛耗吁
可慨也越人如齊夜舍空室而有懌心則
偕五尺豎子因謂之安比盜至無可與謀
===
===
而後知豎子之不足恃吁亦晚矣以今天
下衛兵其不為豎子者寡矣論戰鬪之事
則縮頸而股慄聞盜賊之名則掩耳而不
願聽此其驕惰脆弱誠有如執事所謂類
多耄憊者且其平居坐食未甞經涉險阻
逐隊趨營未甞親交劔楯聰明不足以赴
旗鼓之節强銳不足以犯死傷之地誠有
如執事所謂卒無勇敢者蟻聚於支廩之
司鳥散於辨貌之吏稽籍則存覈實則亡
punctuated:
王尋等百萬之師。苻堅百萬之衆，不能當東晉之三萬；曹操恃其三十萬衆，而敗於吕布，及歸許而悟也，遂能以二萬破袁紹四十萬之衆。此兵多必敗、兵少則勝之明驗也。彼慶曆君臣計不出此，竭天下之財力，浚百姓之膏髓，崇虛名以養無用之兵，卒之國勢日以卑弱，而海內日以虛耗。吁，可慨也！
越人如齊，夜舍空室而有懌心，則偕五尺豎子，因謂之安。比盜至，無可與謀，而後知豎子之不足恃，吁，亦晚矣！
以今天下衛兵，其不為豎子者寡矣。論戰鬪之事，則縮頸而股慄；聞盜賊之名，則掩耳而不願聽。此其驕惰脆弱，誠有如執事所謂類多耄憊者。且其平居坐食，未甞經涉險阻；逐隊趨營，未甞親交劔楯。聰明不足以赴旗鼓之節，强銳不足以犯死傷之地，誠有如執事所謂卒無勇敢者。蟻聚於支廩之司，鳥散於辨貌之吏，稽籍則存，覈實則亡。
translation_en:
…the million-strong army of Wang Xun and the others. Fu Jian’s million troops could not withstand the Eastern Jin’s thirty thousand. Cao Cao relied on his three hundred thousand troops but was defeated by Lü Bu. Upon returning to Xu, he recognized his error and was then able, with twenty thousand men, to defeat Yuan Shao’s four hundred thousand. These are clear proofs that numerous troops mean certain defeat, while few troops bring victory. The ruler and ministers of the Qingli era failed to devise their plans accordingly. They exhausted the empire’s financial resources and drained the common people’s very lifeblood, exalting an empty reputation by maintaining useless troops. In the end, the state grew weaker and more abased by the day, while the realm became ever more depleted. Alas, how lamentable!
A man of Yue traveled to Qi and lodged for the night in an empty room. Feeling apprehensive [?; the transcription reads “pleased”], he took a boy five chi tall as his companion and consequently considered himself safe. When robbers arrived, however, he had no one with whom to devise a plan. Only then did he realize that the boy could not be relied upon. Alas, it was already too late!
Among the guard troops throughout the empire today, few are any different from that boy. When warfare is discussed, they shrink back their necks and their thighs tremble; when they hear bandits mentioned, they cover their ears and refuse to listen. Their arrogance, indolence, frailty, and weakness are indeed just as you describe when you say that most are aged and exhausted. Moreover, in ordinary life they sit idle and eat, never having traversed difficult or dangerous terrain. They follow their units into camp, never having personally crossed swords and shields with an enemy. Their perceptiveness is insufficient to respond to the signals of flags and drums, and their strength and spirit are insufficient to venture where death and injury await. They are indeed just as you describe when you say that the soldiers lack courage. They gather like ants at the office that issues grain allowances, but scatter like birds before the clerks who check their identities by appearance. Examining the registers, one finds them present; checking the actual men, one finds them absent…

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
誠有如執事所謂士多闕伍者開府庫輦
錢鏹得之而不恩一逆其意則欲羣起而
噪呼誠有如執事所謂每稱不足者夫未
嘗不厚其生未嘗不敎之藝未嘗不閱其
數務其實而卒不得其用反虞其害法至
於此弊不可謂不極矣尚可苟安目前冀
旦夕無事持之而不變乎昔者唐之兵蓋
三變矣雖其意有臧否要之事關大計則
不容以不變今欲蘇萬姓之困坐致富强
===
舎兵費之外無可與計者欲省其費莫如
選兵而選兵豈易能哉不歸之農不可也
自少至壯皆已籍之爲兵矣則商賈工技
皆非其有矣則其老而弱也於義不得不
贍之故必如宋建隆咸平之給田可也然
則於何而取田也取之見存之屯也取之
入租之官地也取之籍沒之產也不足則
取之毀廢淫祠之田園也復不足則取之
湖山斥鹵漲沙海蕩之可墾者補之也夫
punctuated: 誠有如執事所謂士多闕伍者。開府庫，輦錢鏹，得之而不恩，一逆其意，則欲羣起而噪呼，誠有如執事所謂每稱不足者。夫未嘗不厚其生，未嘗不敎之藝，未嘗不閱其數、務其實，而卒不得其用，反虞其害。法至於此，弊不可謂不極矣。尚可苟安目前，冀旦夕無事，持之而不變乎？昔者唐之兵蓋三變矣，雖其意有臧否，要之事關大計，則不容以不變。今欲蘇萬姓之困，坐致富强，舎兵費之外，無可與計者。欲省其費，莫如選兵，而選兵豈易能哉？不歸之農，不可也。自少至壯，皆已籍之爲兵矣，則商賈工技皆非其有矣。則其老而弱也，於義不得不贍之。故必如宋建隆、咸平之給田可也。然則於何而取田也？取之見存之屯也，取之入租之官地也，取之籍沒之產也。不足，則取之毀廢淫祠之田園也；復不足，則取之湖山斥鹵、漲沙海蕩之可墾者補之也。夫
translation_en:
… Indeed, this is just as you have said: “Many soldiers are missing from the ranks.” The treasuries are opened and cash is carted out, yet those who receive it feel no gratitude. If their wishes are thwarted even once, they are ready to rise together in an uproar. This is indeed just as you have said: “They constantly complain that it is insufficient.” There has been no failure to provide generously for their livelihood, to teach them military skills, or to review their numbers and ensure that the actual strength matches the rolls. Yet in the end we obtain no service from them and instead fear the harm they may cause. When the system has reached this point, its abuses can only be called extreme. Can we still content ourselves with temporary ease, hope that nothing will happen from one day to the next, and maintain it unchanged?

In former times, the military system of the Tang underwent three transformations. Although the intentions behind them had their merits and faults, the essential point is that when matters concern the great affairs of state, change cannot be avoided. If we now wish to relieve the distress of the people and readily achieve wealth and strength, no reckoning can leave military expenditure out of account. To reduce this expenditure, nothing is better than selecting the troops to be retained. Yet how could such selection be easy? It cannot be done without returning the others to farming. From youth through adulthood they have all been registered as soldiers, so commerce and handicrafts are not skills they possess. Thus, when they become old and weak, we are morally obliged to support them. We must therefore follow the example of the grants of land made during the Jianlong and Xianping reign periods of the Song.

From where, then, should we obtain the land? From military agricultural colonies that still exist; from government lands yielding rental revenue; and from confiscated estates. If these are insufficient, take the fields and gardens of suppressed unauthorized shrines. If these still do not suffice, make up the shortage with reclaimable land around lakes and hills, saline wastelands, newly deposited sandbanks, and coastal flats. Now …

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
屯田之籍不可復也乆矣富豪乾沒猾卒
盜沽自其祖父侵爲己有而子孫固以爲
世業有難以左券捄者故曰取之見存之
屯也蓋失今不察將并其見存之額而亡
之矣今天下官租之地往往而是上不足
以利國祗足爲奸欺之資耳是不可以贍
兵耶籍沒之產未嘗絕書裁價斥賣未足
爲公家之利也以之益屯顧不宜耶梵寺
淫祠以無牒廢者日益於天下而未見公
===
家取以爲利此不可以置屯耶夫遊食之
徒其病農也乆矣今取其田以蘇農民之
困顧不可耶斥鹵閒地之可墾者天下在
在有之以利率人其化瘠土爲沃壤理所
必有夫莫之禁而不爲竊爲執事者病之
執事苟虛心嘉納而求之於
制則是說也非愚臣之臆說也寔成我
祖宗之德而廣其未備也蓋嘗考之
制矣天下郡縣皆有兵以鎮守之亦有屯田以
punctuated:
屯田之籍不可復也乆矣。富豪乾沒，猾卒盜沽，自其祖父侵爲己有，而子孫固以爲世業，有難以左券捄者，故曰取之見存之屯也。蓋失今不察，將并其見存之額而亡之矣。今天下官租之地，往往而是，上不足以利國，祗足爲奸欺之資耳，是不可以贍兵耶？籍沒之產，未嘗絕書，裁價斥賣，未足爲公家之利也；以之益屯，顧不宜耶？梵寺淫祠以無牒廢者，日益於天下，而未見公家取以爲利，此不可以置屯耶？夫遊食之徒，其病農也乆矣。今取其田，以蘇農民之困，顧不可耶？斥鹵閒地之可墾者，天下在在有之。以利率人，其化瘠土爲沃壤，理所必有。夫莫之禁而不爲，竊爲執事者病之。
執事苟虛心嘉納，而求之於制，則是說也，非愚臣之臆說也，寔成我祖宗之德而廣其未備也。蓋嘗考之制矣：天下郡縣皆有兵以鎮守之，亦有屯田以
translation_en:
…The military agricultural colonies’ registered holdings have long been beyond recovery. Wealthy magnates have appropriated them, and unscrupulous soldiers have sold them illicitly. Their forefathers seized these lands as their own, and their descendants now regard them as hereditary property; some are difficult to recover even with documentary proof. Thus I say that land should be taken from the colonies that still survive. If we fail to investigate now, even their remaining registered acreage will be lost.
Land yielding rent to the government is found throughout the realm. It does not adequately benefit the state, serving merely as a resource for fraud and deception. Could it not support the soldiers? Confiscated properties never cease to appear in the records, yet selling them off at reduced prices brings insufficient benefit to the public treasury. Would it not be appropriate to use them to enlarge the colonies? Throughout the realm, increasing numbers of Buddhist temples and unauthorized shrines are being abolished for lack of official certificates, yet we have not seen the government put their property to profitable use. Could agricultural colonies not be established on these lands? Those who live without productive employment have long burdened agriculture. Could we not now take their land to relieve the farmers’ distress? Reclaimable saline wasteland and idle land exist everywhere in the realm. If people are led by the prospect of profit, barren soil will surely be transformed into fertile fields. Nothing prohibits this, yet it goes undone; I humbly regard this as a failing on the part of those in charge.
If those in charge would receive this proposal with an open mind and examine the imperial regulations, they would find that it is no fanciful notion of your ignorant servant. It would indeed fulfill the beneficent purposes of our imperial ancestors and extend what they left incomplete. I have examined the regulations: throughout the realm, prefectures and counties all have troops stationed to defend them, and they also have military agricultural colonies to…

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
廩之以籍軍十分之三服農畝之事二人
受田四十畝歳入十二石足供一兵而自
食其餘餘丁亦以差受田而歳課其入蓋
初非不欲番休迭上盡歸之農顧勢有未
能耳及生齒漸多則地利益盡督屯得人
則歳入益富行之百年則舉天下之屯足
以廩天下之兵矣此立法之意蓋欲待之
將來觀其分數有常置屯無限則可見矣
如此則民之所輸止以供國用耳乃今一
===
兵以上盡仰縣官農夫終歳勤動所賴以
爲生者亦尠矣是豈
祖宗之意哉故爲今日計莫若以前所陳五等
之田每一兵量地腴瘠受田有差使人年
二十則上番爲兵筋力將衰則復歸爲民
撮粒不取於倉寸帛不取於府而吾兵皆
精銳矣或曰一旦變之寧不起怨夫爲之
固有漸次必使之樂於就農固有説也夫
今財賦之地上田二畝價可一金有田十
punctuated: 廩之，以籍軍十分之三服農畝之事，二人受田四十畝，歳入十二石，足供一兵，而自食其餘。餘丁亦以差受田，而歳課其入。蓋初非不欲番休迭上，盡歸之農，顧勢有未能耳。及生齒漸多，則地利益盡；督屯得人，則歳入益富。行之百年，則舉天下之屯，足以廩天下之兵矣。此立法之意，蓋欲待之將來，觀其分數有常，置屯無限，則可見矣。如此，則民之所輸，止以供國用耳。乃今一兵以上，盡仰縣官，農夫終歳勤動，所賴以爲生者亦尠矣。是豈祖宗之意哉？故爲今日計，莫若以前所陳五等之田，每一兵量地腴瘠，受田有差，使人年二十則上番爲兵，筋力將衰則復歸爲民。撮粒不取於倉，寸帛不取於府，而吾兵皆精銳矣。或曰：「一旦變之，寧不起怨？」夫爲之固有漸次，必使之樂於就農，固有説也。夫今財賦之地，上田二畝，價可一金，有田十
translation_en:
…to provision them, assigning three-tenths of the registered soldiers to agricultural work. Every two men received forty mu of land, yielding twelve shi of grain annually, enough to support one soldier while they themselves lived on the remainder. The remaining adult males also received land in varying amounts, and annual levies were assessed on their produce. From the outset, the intention was surely to alternate periods of leave and duty and bring them all into farming; circumstances, however, prevented its full realization. As the population gradually increased, the land’s productive capacity would be more fully exploited; with suitable men supervising the military agricultural colonies, annual yields would grow still greater. After a hundred years of operation, the military agricultural colonies throughout the realm would suffice to provision all its soldiers. The intention behind this legislation was evidently to await these future results. This is apparent from the fixed proportions assigned to cultivation and the absence of any limit on establishing colonies. Under such arrangements, the people’s tax payments would serve only to meet the state’s other expenses. Yet today every soldier depends entirely on the government. Farmers toil throughout the year, with little left on which to subsist. Could this possibly have been the intention of our imperial ancestors?

Thus, in planning for the present, nothing would be better than to use the five grades of land described above, allotting each soldier a different amount according to its fertility or barrenness. At twenty, a man would enter his turn of military service; when his strength began to decline, he would return to civilian status. Not a handful of grain would be drawn from the granaries, nor an inch of silk from the treasuries, yet all our soldiers would be picked and vigorous men.

Someone may ask: “If this were suddenly changed, would it not provoke resentment?” Such a measure would of course proceed by stages, and there are certainly reasons why the men could be made willing to take up farming. Now, in the regions that supply the state’s revenues, two mu of superior land are worth about one liang of silver; possessing ten…

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
畝則爲中人彼兵雖歲入十二石然其自
分固不若中人之産也中人無十二石之
入然終歲出入於一金之中常寛然而有
餘何也不係兵籍則爲商爲工可自慰藉
故歸兵於農乃其所欣慕而爭得之而非
有所厲也怨安從生今夫以百畝之田牧
馬千駟而不知其費聚千駟之馬而輸百
畝之芻則其費百倍此散兵於農之喻至
易曉也固李泰伯之意也以經濟爲任者
===
尚其留意焉
punctuated: 畝則爲中人。彼兵雖歲入十二石，然其自分固不若中人之産也。中人無十二石之入，然終歲出入於一金之中，常寛然而有餘，何也？不係兵籍，則爲商爲工，可自慰藉。故歸兵於農，乃其所欣慕而爭得之，而非有所厲也，怨安從生？今夫以百畝之田牧馬千駟，而不知其費；聚千駟之馬而輸百畝之芻，則其費百倍。此散兵於農之喻，至易曉也，固李泰伯之意也。以經濟爲任者，尚其留意焉！
translation_en: … mu of land makes one a person of middling means. Although those soldiers receive twelve shi of grain annually, they themselves recognize that their lot is certainly inferior to the estate of a person of middling means. Such a person does not receive twelve shi, yet throughout the year his receipts and expenditures remain within a single unit of silver, and he is always comfortably provided for, with something to spare. Why? Because he is not bound to the military registers, he can engage in trade or a craft and thereby provide for his own comfort. Thus, returning soldiers to farming is something they would welcome and compete to obtain; it would cause them no hardship. Whence, then, could resentment arise? Now, if one pastures a thousand teams of horses on a hundred mu of land, one scarcely notices the expense; but if one gathers a thousand teams of horses together and transports to them the fodder from a hundred mu, the expense is a hundred times greater. This analogy for dispersing soldiers among the farming population is exceedingly easy to understand. It is indeed the idea of Li Taibo. May those who take statecraft as their responsibility give it their attention!

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
福建鄉試錄後序
竊聞化之隆也候於遠治之
衰也候於近周文王壽考作
人而汝墳江沱之間至於田
野武夫皆可爲干城腹心及
周之衰則自溱洧之郊密邇
王畿且學校墮壞士人挑闥
===
而缺於禮故詩人本王道之
興廢兎罝子衿竝列於風豈
非以遠近爲候與今閩粤去
畿甸最遙乃士人蔚然有章採
禮樂之華掇仁義之精其經
術直與鄒魯相抗而文采或
過焉於戲此所謂候諸遠者
punctuated:
福建鄉試錄後序

竊聞化之隆也，候於遠；治之衰也，候於近。周文王壽考作人，而汝墳江沱之間，至於田野武夫，皆可爲干城腹心。及周之衰，則自溱洧之郊，密邇王畿，且學校墮壞，士人挑闥而缺於禮。故詩人本王道之興廢，《兎罝》《子衿》竝列於風，豈非以遠近爲候與？今閩粤去畿甸最遙，乃士人蔚然有章，採禮樂之華，掇仁義之精，其經術直與鄒魯相抗，而文采或過焉。於戲！此所謂候諸遠者
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Fujian Provincial Examination

I have humbly heard that the flourishing of moral transformation is discerned in distant regions, while the decline of good government is discerned nearby. King Wen of Zhou lived to a venerable age and nurtured men of worth. In the regions of the banks of the Ru and the Jiang and Tuo rivers, even warriors from the countryside could serve as shields and ramparts and as trusted confidants. When Zhou declined, however, even in the outskirts along the Zhen and Wei rivers, close to the royal domain, schools fell into ruin, and scholars wandered frivolously [?] and were deficient in ritual propriety. Thus the poets, tracing the rise and decline of the Kingly Way, included both “The Rabbit Net” (Tu ju) and “Your Collar” (Zi jin) among the Airs of the States. Was this not because they took conditions far and near as signs?

Today Min-Yue lies farthest from the capital region, yet its scholars display abundant refinement. They gather the blossoms of ritual and music and draw upon the essence of benevolence and righteousness. Their learning in the Classics fully rivals that of Zou and Lu, and their literary accomplishment sometimes surpasses it. Ah! This is what is meant by discerning the signs in distant regions…

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
乎蓋自我
高皇帝取閩時曾不血刃而八郡
嚮風山珍海錯海外奇寶方
軌而走於中國下至蠻谿蜑
壑皆得脫去桴鼓之警而脩
其俎豆之業者且百餘年今
天子又方懋德建中以仁義禮樂
===
鼓鑄區宇漸濡煦沫冒于海
隅是其人文之化鬱於古而
盛於今有不然與說者謂文
王國於岐豐而江沱汝墳正
直其南故詩人歌之謂之二
南言王化自北而究於南今
京師古幽薊之墟當中國艮維
punctuated: 乎？蓋自我高皇帝取閩時，曾不血刃，而八郡嚮風，山珍海錯、海外奇寶，方軌而走於中國。下至蠻谿蜑壑，皆得脫去桴鼓之警，而脩其俎豆之業者，且百餘年。今天子又方懋德建中，以仁義禮樂鼓鑄區宇，漸濡煦沫，冒于海隅。是其人文之化，鬱於古而盛於今，有不然與？說者謂文王國於岐豐，而江沱汝墳正直其南，故詩人歌之，謂之二南，言王化自北而究於南。今京師，古幽薊之墟，當中國艮維，
translation_en:
…is this not so? Ever since our Emperor Gao took Fujian, without so much as bloodying a blade, its eight prefectures turned toward his civilizing influence. Mountain delicacies, the sea’s abundant produce, and rare treasures from overseas streamed into the Central Lands in carts running abreast. Even the Man of the mountain streams and the Dan of the ravines were freed from the alarms of war drums and able to cultivate the practices of ritual worship. This has now continued for more than a hundred years. The present Son of Heaven is further exerting himself in virtue and establishing the mean, molding the realm through benevolence, righteousness, rites, and music. His influence permeates and nurtures all, extending to the shores of the sea. Thus the civilizing influence of letters and culture here, flourishing in antiquity, is still more abundant today. How could it be otherwise?
Commentators say that King Wen established his realm in Qi and Feng, while the Jiang and Tuo rivers and the banks of the Ru lay directly to their south. Hence the poets sang of these places in what are called the Two Southern Sections of the Book of Odes, indicating that royal transformation spread from the north to reach the south. Today the capital occupies the ancient site of You and Ji, at the northeastern corner of the Central Lands…

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
閩粤當巽維亦直其南觀之
天文北極執斗樞以旋轉六
合而閩粤在東甌之宿近太
微明堂之位北直斗柄又大
海首起於東北而其委在東
南潮汐相應天地呼吸之氣
相通由此言之天運人事殆
===
有符應者乎故不以閩粤
之盛爲天下文明之候而不
敢以繫之一方之開塞也夫
多士者不啻古兎罝野人之
儔也既與山珍海錯竝輸於
天子豈不有魁梧瓌偉之器可以
當干城腹心如兎罝野人者
banxin: 福建鄉試錄後序 三
punctuated: 閩粤當巽維，亦直其南。觀之天文，北極執斗樞以旋轉六合，而閩粤在東甌之宿，近太微明堂之位，北直斗柄。又大海首起於東北，而其委在東南，潮汐相應，天地呼吸之氣相通。由此言之，天運人事殆有符應者乎？故不以閩粤之盛爲天下文明之候，而不敢以繫之一方之開塞也。夫多士者，不啻古兎罝野人之儔也。既與山珍海錯竝輸於天子，豈不有魁梧瓌偉之器，可以當干城腹心，如兎罝野人者
translation_en:
…Min and Yue occupy the southeastern quarter, likewise directly to its south. Looking to the celestial patterns, the North Pole holds the pivot of the Dipper, turning the six directions; Min and Yue lie under the asterism of Dong’ou, near the position of Taiwei, the celestial Hall of Light, with the Dipper’s handle directly to their north. Moreover, the great sea originates in the northeast and empties in the southeast. Its tides respond to one another, and the vital breaths of Heaven and Earth communicate. Speaking on this basis, might the movements of Heaven and human affairs indeed correspond? Thus one does not regard [?] the flourishing of Min and Yue as a sign of cultural brilliance throughout the realm, yet does not dare attribute it merely to the opening or obstruction of opportunities in a single region.
These many scholars are no less than the counterparts of the rustic men of antiquity celebrated in “The Rabbit Net.” Since they are presented to the Son of Heaven together with the treasures of the mountains and the delicacies of the sea, surely among them are men of imposing and extraordinary ability who can serve as shields and bulwarks, as trusted confidants, like the rustic men of “The Rabbit Net”…

title: 嘉靖十六年福建鄉試錄
text:
與則世有歌頌
天子作人之化其必以閩粵爲二
南矣多士亦永有聞於世矣
乎
浙江紹興府諸暨縣儒學教
諭尹一仁謹序
punctuated:
與？則世有歌頌天子作人之化，其必以閩粵爲二南矣，多士亦永有聞於世矣乎？
浙江紹興府諸暨縣儒學教諭尹一仁謹序。
translation_en:
…? Then, when people celebrate in song the Son of Heaven’s transforming influence in nurturing men of talent, surely they will regard Min and Yue as the lands of the Two Nan—the Southern Zhou and Southern Shao sections of the Book of Odes—and these many scholars, too, will enjoy lasting renown in the world, will they not?
Preface respectfully composed by Yin Yiren, Instructor at the Confucian School of Zhuji County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang.
